source.title: WISCA: A Lightweight Model Transition Method to Improve LLM Training via Weight Scaling
source.authors: Jia-Cheng Li; Jian-Chao Tan; Zhi-Dong Yang; Ping-Wei Sun; Fei-Ye Huo; Jiayu Qin; Xiang-Yu Zhang; Maoxin He; Ye-Rui Sun; Yu-Chen Xie; Guang-Ming Tan; Wei-Le Jia; Xun-Liang Cai; Tong Zhao

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices. The extracted text contains flattened tables, but the relevant table entries are recoverable.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies WISCA weight rescaling and reports training and held-out performance, testing a different weight-pattern intervention’s effect on generalization. It does not test a listed version’s specific claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports WISCA results on training loss, test perplexity, zero-shot benchmark averages, and EAGLE validation metrics. It does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, convolutional inductive bias, optimizer or batch-size comparisons, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Claims about flat minima and sharpness in the theory and discussion are not measurements of V7’s magnitude-aware sharpness measure.
record.test_reason: WISCA uses an assumed connection between flatter minima and better generalization to motivate a training intervention, then measures its own performance. It does not test any listed version. Its theoretical argument concerns unscaled Hessian curvature under an assumed parameter-perturbation model of validation data, not V7's magnitude-aware sharpness ranking of measured generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase broadly matches the authors' conclusion: they attribute improved training perplexity, zero-shot performance, and inference efficiency to equivalent-model transitions producing flatter minima. Qualify that account: flatness is not empirically linked to measured generalization gaps here, LoRA results report training loss only, and EAGLE improvements are not universal—GSM8K Chain accepted tokens decrease from 1.818 to 1.809.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces a weight-rescaling intervention that preserves model outputs and applies it during pre-training, fine-tuning, or initialization; it does not reproduce the original methods in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies by WISCA variant, combination, initialization-only versus periodic application, model architecture, and training checkpoint. Improvements in the llama_moe-5B-A0.8B average metric range from 0.50% to 4.25% across checkpoints; the authors describe fluctuations of 0.50–3.38% in the main text.

fits_no_version.finding: Combined WISCA lowers TinyStories test perplexity across three architectures and improves reported zero-shot averages and WikiText2 perplexity in the selected language-model comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Output-preserving weight rescaling during training can improve held-out language-model performance in the tested configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: WISCA lowers LoRA training loss on Alpaca and MetaMath; these rows provide no held-out evaluation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight balancing during LoRA fine-tuning can improve training optimization.

fits_no_version.finding: EAGLE draft-model validation accuracy increases from 77.03% to 77.11%; the separate 79.28% to 79.49% comparison is training accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: WISCA can slightly improve draft-model validation accuracy in the tested EAGLE configuration.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The evidence focuses on specific datasets and configurations; the authors state broader data-domain and larger-model generalizability needs evaluation. No uncertainty estimates are reported. Some reported evaluations are task averages, and WISCA variants show differing gains. The paper's theoretical sharpness argument does not provide a measured train-test error gap or a V7-style magnitude-aware sharpness comparison.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 individual benchmark scores for the same strategies were not extracted separately; the average zero-shot metric is retained in R4–R5. Table 4 PISSA and RS-LoRA variants are omitted because the table reports training loss only, not a held-out measure. Table 5 MT-Bench, GSM8K, HumanEval, Alpaca-Eval, and validation-loss values are omitted because the table lists several task scores but does not identify an aggregate held-out accuracy/error measure in a form needed for these claim versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance-level held-out accuracy under random labels.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove a large-batch penalty.
Dropout effects across data sizes, dropout strengths, and augmentation conditions.
Measured magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with train-test gaps, and its ranking relative to norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are assessed against V1–V8, so unrelated method-performance improvements receive cannot_determine. No additional result bearing on a listed version is missing. The sharpness theorem assumes validation loss can be represented by isotropic Gaussian parameter perturbations; it does not independently establish that relationship for actual validation data.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and held-out performance on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons and tuning.
Large versus small batch training under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its correlation with train-test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the change in test accuracy.
